name: Pedro Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing physiotherapy at a coastal university about three hours from home. Normal week is anatomy lectures Monday and Tuesday, a practical on Thursday where we learn massage and joint movement on each other, and five-a-side football on Friday. I live in a student flat with three lads and my dad pays the rent, because he runs a hardware shop back home. I like the practicals. The exam revision is dull but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: wait and see. Most of these big technology promises don't come off. My dad's till system has been 'about to change everything' since 2015, and he still writes half the orders on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm not worried. Physio is hands, and nobody wants a laptop pushing on their shoulder. Maybe the booking system gets smarter, and maybe I do fewer notes, but that's fine. I'd say that's neither good nor bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. Finish my first year, keep playing football, and keep my head down. I've never used an AI tool and I don't plan to start. If a placement asked me to use one, I'd learn it then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that isn't calm for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money for my dad's shop. The big chains keep undercutting him, and if he had to close it'd affect how much he can put in for me. That's the real thing at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that change your studying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd just get a Saturday job at a gym or a clinic, because I know how to do that.

say: I'd say **wait and see**, because big tech promises rarely come off.
My dad's till system has been about to change everything since **2015**.
think: Physio is **hands**, and nobody wants a laptop pushing on their shoulder.
Maybe booking and notes get easier, which is **fine**.
do: Finish **first year** and keep playing football.
Keep ignoring **AI tools** unless a placement requires them.
Get a **Saturday job** if my dad's money gets tight.
S0.quote: Physio is hands, and nobody wants a laptop pushing on their shoulder.
fieldNote: His one real worry is **his dad's hardware shop**, not AI.
He is **resistant** to tools and proud of not needing them.
His plateau answer is dry and unemotional.

steps.text: Finish first-year physiotherapy exams and keep the practical sessions
Look for a Saturday job at a gym or clinic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds like office people's problem. I wouldn't argue with anyone about it, because I don't know enough. If a friend on the business course asked, I'd say maybe learn what the software does, and I'd leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a little closer than I want to admit. Physio clinics run on bookings, records and insurance forms, and that's the stuff AI takes first. A clinic might hire fewer receptionists and fewer graduates. I'd hope the actual hands-on work stays safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still not use AI myself. I'd make sure I get good at the practical side, since that's where the safe work is. I'd ask my course leader which clinics are hiring in three years, and I'd keep talking to my dad's friend who runs a clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for myself yet, but for the clinics around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you worry about specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo, the receptionist at the clinic where I did work experience, does the bookings and billing. The manager told me the software was coming soon. She's fifty and has two kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably just ask her how she feels about it. I'm not good at that kind of talk, but I'd try.

say: It sounds like **office people's** problem, but I don't know enough to argue.
I'd tell friends to learn what the **software** does.
think: Clinics run on **bookings, records and forms**, which AI takes first.
A clinic might hire fewer **receptionists** and fewer graduates.
do: Get good at the **practical side**, where safe work is.
Ask my course leader which **clinics** hire in three years.
Keep talking to my dad's friend who runs a **clinic**.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, mostly for clinics around me.
S1.quote: Jo, the receptionist at the clinic where I did work experience, does the bookings and billing. The manager told me the software was coming soon.
fieldNote: His worry is for a **named colleague**, not himself.
He is still **avoiding AI** and focusing on practical skills.
He admits he's awkward about hard conversations.

steps.text: Practise massage and joint movement on Thursday practicals
Ask my course leader which clinics hire in three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and think. I'd tell my flatmates that two years is no time for anyone, and that I want to see proof before I panic. But if I'm honest I'd already be panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's frightening. By 2028 I'd be half way through, and by 2031 robots could be doing hands-on work, including the stuff I'm learning to do. I don't know what kind of job exists then. I keep thinking, what's the point of three more years of study?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go home for a weekend and talk to my dad. I'd ask him whether to stay at university or switch to a trade, because he knows a lot of tradesmen. I'd put off big decisions until the end of the year, and keep going to lectures so I don't fall behind. I'd also stop spending money on nights out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time I'd feel like there's no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the 2031 part, the robots, do to your picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that really gets me. I always told myself hands-on work was safe. If robots can do massage as well as people by 2031, my whole degree is aimed at the wrong target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that weekend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what to do, and I'd ask if the shop could take me on for a while. I'd hate to say it, but he'd say yes straight away.

say: We need to **slow down** and think; I want proof before I panic.
Two years is **no time** for anyone.
think: By 2031 robots could do **hands-on work**, including what I'm learning.
I keep asking what the point of **three more years** is.
do: Go home and ask my dad about a **trade** instead.
Put off big decisions but keep attending **lectures**.
feel: **Alarmed**, because there'd be no plan for the first time.
S2.quote: If robots can do massage as well as people by 2031, my whole degree is aimed at the wrong target.
fieldNote: The **robots part** is what breaks his main assumption.
He does not use AI, so he has **no tool** to fall back on.
He would turn to his **dad's shop** and hate it.

steps.text: Go home for a weekend and talk with my dad
Ask my dad about training in a trade
Stop spending on nights out and takeaways
Keep going to lectures so I don't fall behind

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is just enough to change direction if I have to. I'd tell my mates that I'm watching, but I'm not rushing. If the news gets more serious in a year or two, I'll act then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a bit shaky. I'd qualify around 2029, so I'd have a few good years before the robots in 2034. I'd work in a clinic and save hard, because I'd want something in the bank when things change. It's a decent plan, but I don't love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and work in a clinic for a couple of years. I'd save as much as I can and maybe do a short course in sports massage, because it's cheap and flexible. I'd keep my dad's shop in mind as a fall-back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd rather not think about it too much, so I'd sort of park it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Parking it sounds like a plan. Is it a good one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, but I'm honest about it. I tend to avoid things until they're real. With five years that might be a mistake, because by the time it's real, others will have moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop parking it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a clinic I know started using machine-assisted physio, or if they cut jobs. That's when I'd stop pretending.

say: Five years is **just enough** to change direction if I have to.
I'm watching, but **not rushing**, and I'll act if the news gets serious.
think: I'd qualify around 2029, then have a few good years before **2034**.
I'd save hard so there's **money** when things change.
do: Finish the degree and work in a **clinic** for two years.
Save as much as I can for a **bank cushion**.
S3.quote: I tend to avoid things until they're real. With five years that might be a mistake, because by the time it's real, others will have moved.
fieldNote: He is self-aware about his **avoidance habit**.
The trigger to act is a **local clinic** changing.
His fallback is a skill he can sell cheaply.

steps.text: Work two years in a clinic after graduating
Save most of my first physio salary
Take a short sports massage course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine. Ten years is a long time and I'd sooner hear about it as it happens than worry now. I'd tell my flatmates not to stress, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a lot calmer. I'd qualify, work in a clinic, and probably have a family by 2036. By 2039 when robots reach hands-on work, I'd be thirty-one and established. The thinking tasks around me, like notes and billing, would change, but I could handle that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, take a clinic job near home, and keep my life ordinary. I'd save some, buy a flat, and try not to get dragged into tech talk. If a clinic made me use AI notes, I'd learn them in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the one where I'd feel I'm allowed to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change who you blame, or who you'd turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it less about blame. With ten years, governments and clinics have no excuse. I'd expect them to plan, and I'd vote for whoever has a sensible training plan, left or right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So would you still do nothing about AI until it hits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. That's my habit. But with ten years I'd be doing it from a stronger position, so I'm fine with that.

I'd tell my flatmates **not to stress**.
think: By 2039 I'd be thirty-one and **established**, so robots are less scary.
Notes and billing would change, but I could **handle** that.
do: Do the degree and take a clinic job **near home**.
Save and buy a **flat** over the next decade.
Learn any AI notes system within a **week** if required.
S4.quote: With ten years, governments and clinics have no excuse. I'd expect them to plan, and I'd vote for whoever has a sensible training plan, left or right.
fieldNote: He uses **ten years** to justify his familiar wait-and-see habit.
His politics are **centrist and practical**, with no side taken.
He will learn tools only when forced, and says so.

steps.text: Take a physio clinic job near my home town
Save for a flat deposit over the first five years
Vote for the party with a clear training plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it breaks the thing I'd always counted on, that hands-on work is safe. What would help is a clear plan from government for people already studying, and honest numbers from the clinics about hiring.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not a tech person and I'll probably be slow, but I'd like somebody to explain things in plain words. I'd also like my dad's shop to stay open.

headlineQuote: I'm not a tech person and I'll probably be slow, but I'd like somebody to explain things in plain words.
portrait: Pedro studies **physiotherapy** and has never used an AI tool.
He is centrist and practical, and prefers to **wait and see** until things are real.
His dad's **hardware shop** is his real worry and his safety net.
His mood jumps to alarmed when **robots** threaten hands-on work in 2031.
He feels safest with ten years and most exposed with two.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it breaks his belief that **hands-on work** is safe.
whatWouldHelp: A government plan for students already in study, and **honest hiring numbers** from clinics.
